name: Looksmax.org / forum participation

card.summary: The main forum hub of looksmaxxing culture, where members post progress photos, seek PSL ratings and swap guides.
card.note: Community norms include PSL ratings and unverified methods; researchers and media have raised mental health and radicalisation concerns.

quick.overview:
Looksmax.org is described as one of the main later hubs of looksmaxxing, alongside forum.looksmaxxing.com. Members post guides, request ratings and share progress photos, often giving a current and 'potential' PSL score.

The forum scene traces back to mid-2010s boards such as Lookism.net and Sluthate, and moved to independent forums after platform bans, before spreading to TikTok around 2020.
quick.mechanism: Participation typically means posting photos for rating, discussing softmaxxing (non-invasive changes) and hardmaxxing (surgery, steroids), and using shared vocabulary such as canthal tilt and hunter eyes. Anonymity is common and members gatekeep against casual 'normies'.
quick.risks: Commentators and researchers link the subculture to body dysmorphia, depression and anxiety, promotion of unproven or dangerous methods, blackpill determinism, and radicalisation. Critics also call the PSL scale unscientific and biased against non-white men.

lead: Looksmax.org is an online forum devoted to improving male appearance, and is described as one of the main hubs of looksmaxxing alongside forum.looksmaxxing.com.[2] Members use it to get feedback on how they look and to find guides on what to change: they post photos for rating threads, track progress photos over months, and read or write guides covering skincare, grooming, hair, fitness, posture and, for some, surgery and medical treatments.[1][2]

Looksmaxxing took shape on message boards in the 2010s. Wikipedia names PUAHate, Sluthate and Lookism.net, now defunct, as the 'PSL forums' that devised the PSL rating scale of facial attractiveness, and notes that male content creators popularized the practice on TikTok in the early 2020s.[1] Looksmax.org itself is a later forum; Female-oriented guides reportedly appeared on it in 2024 and 2025.[2]

The forum has published its own member surveys. Its 2025 survey, reporting on respondents with fewer than 1,000 posts (1,593 responses), found about 62 percent under 18 and roughly 90 percent under 21, with about 99.5 percent identifying as male.[3] Commentators and researchers have also raised concerns about the wider subculture, which are covered below.

chain: Post photos and questions to the community
Receive ratings, critiques and guides on skin, hair, grooming, fitness or surgery
Apply changes and post progress photos
angle.text: Members use the forum as a source of outside feedback and of how-to guides on appearance, and as a place to document progress. Any change in looks comes from the practices members adopt after reading, rather than from posting itself.

paras: Looksmaxxing took shape on incel-linked boards in the mid-2010s.[1][2] After Reddit banned r/incels in 2017, activity moved to independent forums, often on .is domains, and from around 2020 to TikTok, where it reached non-incel audiences.[2] Wikipedia describes early TikTok videos as often presenting looksmaxxing as self-improvement with self-deprecating humor, with black pill ideology becoming more associated with it in mainstream discourse by the mid-2020s.[1]

Looksmax.org has run its own TikTok account, an announcement that drew mixed reactions from members in a forum thread, some of whom said the move would make the forum more mainstream.[4] Members have also compared the forum with its Discord server, with some describing the Discord as rating-focused.[5]

Members post progress photos and request ratings on current and potential PSL, sometimes using wet-hair photos to reduce styling effects.[2] Ratings are competitive and quantify perceived genetic potential.[2] Anonymity is common, and members gatekeep against casual 'normies'.[2] Core vocabulary includes softmaxxing (non-invasive changes such as skincare, grooming and fitness), hardmaxxing (surgery, drugs and other invasive measures), blackpill, canthal tilt, hunter eyes, mewing and bonesmashing.[1][2]

The forum's 2025 survey summary, posted by its administrators, reported that most respondents were very young and almost entirely male, with about 42 percent between 170 and 179 cm tall and about 39 percent between 180 and 189 cm, and North America the largest region.[3] Earlier annual survey threads exist for 2024, and the forum has marked anniversaries with community events.[6][7]

Commentators describe the practice as judgemental and link it to body dysmorphia and suicidal ideation, and researchers say it promotes hegemonic masculinity.[1] Wikipedia also reports that researchers say TikTok algorithms can draw young men toward incel views, that doctors have criticized mewing and bonesmashing as misinformation, and that some men report benefits such as improved confidence or relationships.[1]

Grokipedia lists controversies including blackpill determinism, misogynistic slang, promotion of unproven methods such as bonesmashing and unregulated overseas surgery with reported complications, criticism of PSL as unscientific, and research linking the subculture to radicalisation.[2]
No studies found. Published research on online health and appearance forums in general, such as analyses of weight-loss subreddits and drug-use forums, concerns other communities.[8]

timeline.event: Looksmaxxing forms on incel-linked boards such as Lookism.net and Sluthate.[1][2]
Reddit bans r/incels, pushing activity to independent forums.[2]
Looksmax.org publishes a community survey; female-oriented guides reportedly begin appearing around this time.[2][6]
Looksmax.org publishes another survey of its members.[3]
